passage: The recruiter's office in Toronto smelled of coffee and new carpet. Clara slid the offer across the desk. "We have many candidates for this role," she said. "If you can sign today, it's yours." Kaito's stomach tightened. He liked the job, and he could hear the clock. But he noticed how quickly the line had arrived, before he had read a single page. "Could you email me the terms in writing? I would like to read them tonight and reply tomorrow morning." Clara's smile thinned. "I can't hold it for long." "Understood," Kaito said, pleasantly. "Tomorrow by ten." On the train home he felt shaky, but also strangely calm, as if he had put one foot back on the ground. The email came an hour later.

qa.q: In which city was the recruiter's office?
qa.a: The recruiter's office was in Toronto.

qa.q: Why did Kaito's stomach tighten when Clara told him to sign today?
qa.a: He felt rushed and pressured, because he liked the job but was being asked to decide before reading any pages.

qa.q: What could Kaito do when the written terms arrive?
qa.a: He can read them carefully that evening, note any questions, and reply the next morning, knowing a real offer should survive a day.

qa.q: How might Clara have seen Kaito's request?
qa.a: Clara's smile thinned, so she may have felt pushed against her plan, or worried about other candidates. A real recruiter can still accept a reasonable request for time.

grounding: A recruiter says 'we have many candidates, sign today'; the protagonist feels rushed and asks for the terms in writing and time to decide.

passage: Raghav, the man on the phone says sign today or lose it? Let your Pradeep-chacha tell you about my first job. I was twenty-two, and an agency in Nehru Place offered me a sales post. The manager slid a paper across the desk. 'Many boys are waiting outside. Sign now.' My hands were sweating; I wanted that job badly. But my old headmaster once told me, 'A real offer can wait one night.' So I said, 'Please give me the terms to take home. I'll come back tomorrow at ten.' He frowned and said the seat might go. I went home anyway. That night my elder sister read the paper with me under the tube light. Page two said I'd have to repay three months' salary if I left within two years. Nobody had mentioned that. I went back at ten and asked about it. The seat was still there, and they struck the clause out. So, Raghav: ask for it in writing, and sleep on it.

qa.a: The agency was in Nehru Place.

qa.q: How did young Pradeep feel when the manager said 'Sign now'?
qa.a: Pradeep felt rushed and anxious, his hands sweating because he wanted the job badly.

qa.q: What turning point in the story protected Pradeep?
qa.a: Asking to take the terms home and reading them with his sister, which uncovered a clause nobody had mentioned.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's sister have felt reading page two?
qa.a: His sister likely felt alarmed and protective, glad they had read it before he signed.

grounding: An uncle recalls being pushed to sign on the spot, and how asking for the terms in writing and a night to read them revealed a hidden clause.

passage: At 6:15 on a Friday evening, with the office cleaners already mopping around her feet, Vandana got the call. Abhinav, a recruiter for a Chennai fintech firm, sounded cheerful and fast. 'Great news, you're selected. I'll send the e-sign link now. We have many candidates, so please sign by eight tonight.' Her phone battery was at eleven percent, her bus was in twenty minutes, and her heart was pounding. She wanted to say yes before anything changed. Instead she took a breath. 'Thank you, I'm really happy. Could you email me the full offer letter with the salary break-up, notice period and joining date? I'll read it over the weekend and reply by Monday noon.' A pause. 'Other candidates are waiting.' 'I understand. If the offer is real, I think it can wait till Monday.' He said he'd check. The letter arrived at 7:40. She read it twice on the bus, and on Monday asked one question about probation before signing.

qa.q: By what time did Abhinav ask Vandana to sign?
qa.a: Abhinav asked her to sign by eight tonight.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she got the call?
qa.a: Vandana felt excited but rushed and pressured, wanting to say yes before anything changed.

qa.q: Why was asking for the full letter and time a wise move?
qa.a: A real offer survives a weekend; having the terms in writing let her read them and ask about probation before committing.

qa.q: How does Abhinav try to shape Vandana's decision?
qa.a: Abhinav uses urgency and the threat of other candidates to push a quick signature before she has read the terms.

grounding: Shows a recruiter pressing Vandana to sign the same evening, and her asking for the terms in writing and time to read them.
